beats.text: Torvalds did not walk away from BitKeeper. BitKeeper's maker banned him.
The Linux kernel began using BitKeeper, a proprietary version control tool, over objections from Richard Stallman and a refusal from veteran developer Alan Cox.
beats.note: BitKeeper's free licence for open source developers forbade them from working on any rival tool, including CVS or Subversion, for as long as they used it.

beats.name: Andrew Tridgell
beats.role: An OSDL developer working on an unrelated project. His attempt to view BitKeeper's revision history without paying for a licence gave BitMover its reason to end free use.

beats.text: BitMover did not just shut Tridgell out. It refused to give or sell a licence to anyone employed by OSDL, including Linus Torvalds, who had no part in Tridgell's work.
beats.note: Free use officially ended on 1 July 2005. The Git project began that same year, built to replace BitKeeper for the kernel.

beats.name: Bryan O'Sullivan
beats.role: An employee at a company paying for a commercial BitKeeper licence. In October 2005 he agreed to stop contributing to the rival tool Mercurial after BitMover's founder complained.

beats.line: A dispute mostly about one outside developer ended up creating the tool that now runs almost all of software.
